label: AI Governance in Financial Crime
description: Governance and control framework for AI/ML used in financial-crime systems (transaction monitoring, screening, fraud, KYC) at the intersection of the AMLR risk-based approach, DORA ICT governance, and EU AI Act Title III high-risk requirements.

guidedInputs.label: Institution Type
guidedInputs.description: What type of obliged entity deploys the AI/ML system?

options.label: RegTech / AI Vendor (provider role under the AI Act)

guidedInputs.label: AI/ML Use Case(s)
guidedInputs.description: Where is the AI/ML applied across the financial-crime control stack?

options.label: Transaction Monitoring — alert generation / scenario scoring
Sanctions / PEP / adverse-media name screening (fuzzy matching)
KYC / identity verification / document & biometric checks
Network / graph analytics, perpetual KYC, segmentation

guidedInputs.label: Model Provenance
guidedInputs.description: Who built and trains the model? Determines the provider vs deployer split under EU AI Act Art. 16/26.

options.label: Third-party vendor, no model access (we are deployer)
Vendor model, tuned/retrained on our data (shared provider duties)
Foundation / GPAI model via API (e.g. for GenAI assist)

guidedInputs.label: Jurisdiction(s)
guidedInputs.description: Which regimes apply to the deployment?

guidedInputs.label: Assessment Focus
guidedInputs.description: Which AI-governance control domains should the analysis prioritise?

options.label: Data & data governance / bias sources (AI Act Art. 10)
Technical documentation & model documentation (AI Act Art. 11 + Annex IV)
Vendor / third-party AI assurance (DORA + AI Act Art. 25/26)
Regulatory AI-sandbox engagement readiness (AI Act Art. 57–61)

guidedInputs.label: Known Issues or Concerns
guidedInputs.description: Describe the model lifecycle status, any audit/validation findings, oversight gaps, or supervisory feedback on the AI system.
guidedInputs.placeholder: e.g. ML alert-scoring model retrained quarterly but no documented bias test; investigators trust the score and rarely override (automation-bias risk); vendor will not disclose features; no AI inventory mapping use cases to AI Act risk tiers; SAR rationale cannot reference which model signals drove the alert.

exampleInput: We are a Swedish bank (~2,400 staff, full AMLR scope, directly DORA-regulated) that replaced our legacy rules-only transaction-monitoring engine with a supervised-ML alert-scoring model from a RegTech vendor. The model ranks alerts 0-100 and our level-1 team auto-closes everything below 30; roughly 65% of alerts are now suppressed before a human sees them. The model is retrained quarterly on our investigators' disposition labels. Compliance is worried we cannot explain to Finansinspektionen why a given customer's alert was suppressed, the vendor will not share the feature list ('proprietary'), and we have never run a bias or disparate-impact test across customer segments. We also use a GenAI assistant (foundation model via API) to draft SAR narratives. Assess our AI governance against EU AI Act Title III high-risk requirements, AMLR risk-based-approach and record-keeping obligations, and DORA ICT third-party governance — and tell us what we must fix before the AI Act high-risk obligations bite in August 2026 and before our next FI inspection. We have no AI system inventory and no documented human-oversight model for the auto-closure threshold.

exampleValues.known_concerns: ML alert-scoring model auto-closes ~65% of alerts below score 30 with no human review; no documented human-oversight model for the threshold (automation-bias risk). Vendor will not disclose features ('proprietary'), blocking explainability and model documentation. No bias / disparate-impact test ever run. GenAI SAR-drafting assistant on a foundation model with no logging of prompts/outputs. No AI system inventory mapping use cases to AI Act risk tiers.
